questions.stem: Think it over: Curtis Duarte is setting up a retirement account and asks why naming a beneficiary matters. What is the main reason?

options.text: It guarantees the account will earn a higher return.
options.misconception: treats a designation as an investment feature

options.text: It lowers the amount of annual contribution that is allowed.

options.text: It directs who receives the account and can avoid probate delays.

questions.learningObjective: Apply charitable giving and gifting concepts to realistic financial decisions
questions.stem: A quick scenario: Leila Fontaine plans to make a sizable annual gift to a relative and asks about gift tax treatment. What is the key idea?

options.text: Gifts up to an annual exclusion per recipient generally are not reportable.

options.misconception: confuses a transfer with taxable income

options.text: Only gifts of cash count, never gifts of property.

questions.subject: PERSONAL_FINANCE
questions.learningObjective: Apply charitable giving and gifting concepts to realistic financial decisions
questions.stem: Work through this: Liam Osei receives $600 of monthly income and spends $90 on groceries. What percentage of income is that?

options.misconception: divides the whole by the part instead of the part by the whole
forgets to multiply the fraction by one hundred
reports the dollar amount rather than the percentage share

questions.explanation: The share is the part divided by the whole, then multiplied by one hundred. $90 divided by $600 is 0.15 as a decimal, so 15% of income goes to groceries. Dividing the other way or skipping the factor of one hundred gives a different, wrong figure.
questions.hint: Divide the expense by income, then convert to a percent.

questions.learningObjective: Apply charitable giving and gifting concepts to realistic financial decisions
questions.stem: In practice: Beatriz Okafor receives $660 of monthly income and spends $165 on a phone plan. What percentage of income is that?

options.misconception: reports the dollar amount rather than the percentage share
forgets to multiply the fraction by one hundred
divides the whole by the part instead of the part by the whole

questions.explanation: The share is the part divided by the whole, then multiplied by one hundred. $165 divided by $660 is 0.25 as a decimal, so 25% of income goes to a phone plan. Dividing the other way or skipping the factor of one hundred gives a different, wrong figure.
questions.hint: Divide the expense by income, then convert to a percent.

questions.stem: The decision: A filer in the 25% bracket compares a $2,800 tax credit with a $2,800 tax deduction. Which statement about their effect is accurate?

options.misconception: conflates a credit with a deduction as if both were dollar-for-dollar

options.text: Neither provision changes the amount of tax that is owed.
options.misconception: denies that either a credit or a deduction affects tax

options.text: The deduction is always larger because it uses the tax rate.

questions.stem: A quick scenario: A filer in the 10% bracket compares a $2,700 tax credit with a $2,700 tax deduction. Which statement about their effect is accurate?

options.text: Both provisions reduce the tax bill by the same dollar amount.
options.misconception: conflates a credit with a deduction as if both were dollar-for-dollar

options.text: Neither provision changes the amount of tax that is owed.
options.misconception: denies that either a credit or a deduction affects tax

options.text: The deduction is always larger because it uses the tax rate.
options.misconception: assumes multiplying by a rate below one makes a larger saving

options.text: The credit cuts tax by $2,700; the deduction saves about $270.

questions.explanation: A tax credit reduces tax dollar for dollar, so it cuts $2,700. A deduction reduces taxable income, saving $2,700 times 10%, or about $270. Treating the two as identical or as ineffective misses this distinction.
questions.hint: Credits subtract from tax; deductions subtract from taxable income.
